scope_note: Full-source boundary-date probe of ten Darwin-authored Nature publications. Complete retained bodies, source roles, quoted/reporting voices, dates and apparatus were checked; no incoming prompt is reconstructed and no links are accepted.

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: Darwin’s published Nature intervention addresses Galton’s rabbit blood transfusion experiments. He corrects the premise that Pangenesis requires gemmules in blood, distinguishing diffusion through tissues from circulation, then argues Galton’s negative result does not yet deliver a “death blow” because reproductive elements in blood were never proved. The letter is a signed two-paragraph argument, not Galton’s incoming text.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Galton’s paper was read 30 March 1871; the Nature publication fixes the displayed before-date at 27 April 1871. XML spans 1809-01-01 to 1871-04-26, an open lower metadata bound.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin voice throughout; Galton is quoted and discussed as the experimenter. Bence Jones and Paget are cited as earlier examples, all reported or bibliographic material.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The quoted Galton paper and prior consultation are referenced, but no Galton-to-Darwin prompt is preserved here; the publication response cannot be converted into a surviving direct pair.

evidence.quote: These experiments were undertaken to test whether there was any truth in my provisional hypothesis of Pangenesis
Pangenesis has, as yet, received its death blow

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: Darwin introduces Huggins’s account of inherited antipathy in a dog across three generations. He frames it against instinct acquired by habit, Spalding’s newly hatched birds, tumbling pigeons, and island birds, while allowing sudden useful variations and unknown origins. The surviving text is Darwin’s publication cover and contextual argument; Huggins’s actual letter follows only as an editorially described source, not as body text here.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published in Nature 13 February 1873; XML spans 1809-01-01 to 1873-02-12 and the displayed date is before 13 February 1873.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin wrote the framing prose. Huggins’s dog case, Spalding, Bartlett, and other authorities are quoted/reported voices, not Darwin-authored observations.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Huggins letter and any covering exchange are not preserved in this record, so the publication notice is not a recoverable incoming prompt.

evidence.quote: I have obtained permission from Dr. Huggins to send it for publication
many special fears, tastes, &c., which must have been acquired at a remote period, are now strictly inherited

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: Darwin replies publicly to interest in Wallace’s suggestion that animals navigate home by odour. He supplies a personal mail-coach anecdote: the coachman used a particular wheeler as a route marker at public houses, and Darwin extends the observation to animal perception. The source is a short signed Nature note with a title and no preserved Wallace letter.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published 13 March 1873; XML spans 1809-01-01 to 1873-03-12, displayed before 13 March 1873.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin’s coach anecdote and argument are his voice; Wallace’s suggestion is explicitly reported, not an extant Wallace-to-Darwin text.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Wallace’s original suggestion is unlocated in this source and no direct correspondence prompt is preserved.

evidence.quote: Many years ago I was on a mail-coach
Mr. Wallace’s suggestion that animals find their way home

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: Darwin answers a Nature article on instinct in nine blocks. He defends independent variation as a source of instincts, compares involuntary reflexes and neuter insects, revisits tumbler pigeons, then separates the article’s treatment of homing from his own evidence: Von Wrangell’s Siberian travellers and a remembered Audubon wild goose account. The final paragraphs openly mark memory and missing books, limiting the evidential status of those examples.
record_reviews.date_assessment: The displayed before-date is 3 April 1873, fixed by publication; XML bounds are 1809-01-01 to 1873-04-02.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin is the author; the unnamed Nature writer is summarized and quoted as a third-party interlocutor. Von Wrangell and Audubon are reported sources, with the Audubon passage expressly from memory.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Nature article and any author correspondence are not preserved as a distinct incoming letter; reported works do not establish a direct prompt endpoint.

evidence.quote: The writer of the interesting article in Nature of March 20 doubts whether my belief
I am forced to quote from memory, as I have not my books at hand

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: The first three blocks are Darwin’s introduction to Hague’s ant report; blocks 4–14 reproduce Hague’s detailed observation. Ants approaching dead or disabled nestmates retreat, communicate the danger, later avoid the original vase, and shift to another tumbler where the experiment is repeated. Hague’s final blocks describe prospectors and the abandoned lower colony; the source closes with Hague’s name and San Francisco dateline. This mixed author/embedded report is a publication composite, not a single Darwin observation.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Darwin’s cover is before 3 April 1873; the embedded Hague letter is dated San Francisco 26 February 1873. XML bounds cover 1809-01-01 to 1873-04-02; the embedded dateline is the strongest internal date for Hague’s report.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin writes P1–3; Hague writes P4–16. Darwin’s “distinguished geologist” attribution and the embedded signature/dateline preserve the role boundary.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Hague’s incoming letter is represented inside this publication, but no separate cover or Darwin-to-Hague prompt survives in the record; the publication itself is not a new direct reply.

evidence.quote: has been sent to me by a distinguished geologist, Mr. J. D. Hague
the two would always communicate, but each would pursue its own way

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: Darwin reports a follow-up experiment prompted by Hague’s earlier ant account. Moggridge had heard an Australian anecdote about a finger across an ant path; he repeated the experiment at Mentone. Darwin says he sent Moggridge’s observation to Hague and asked whether smell or sight explained the avoidance, then presents Hague’s confirming letter without reproducing that letter’s body in the retained blocks. This establishes a research chain but leaves the actual Hague response text unavailable here.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published before 24 July 1873; XML bounds are 1809-01-01 to 1873-07-23. The supplied date is publication-based and does not identify when Darwin sent the query or received Hague’s confirmation.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin narrates the chain. Moggridge and the unnamed Australian informant are reported; “Mr. Hague’s letter” is announced as following, but the retained body does not provide its blocks.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The confirming Hague text and the earlier Darwin request are missing as separate endpoint records, so no direct link is proposed.

evidence.quote: I therefore sent the letter to Mr. Hague, and asked him to observe whether his ants were alarmed by the smell left by the finger
Here follows Mr. Hague’s letter, fully confirming his former statement.

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: Darwin presents Fritz Müller’s report on a frog carrying eggs on its back and on reduction or disappearance of caddis-fly leg hairs. He treats the latter as a striking case of disuse under changed conditions, then applies Delbœuf’s law through Murphy’s quoted condensation and connects the argument to earlier Müller letters. The retained blocks end in Darwin’s introduction and quotation setup; the complete Müller letter is not present as body text.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published before 20 March 1879; XML bounds are 1809-01-01 to 1879-03-19. The heading and publication date do not prove the date Darwin received or read Müller’s letter.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin provides the framing text; Müller’s observations and Murphy’s quoted mathematical statement are embedded third-party voices, with later editorial references kept separate.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The specific Müller letter(s) supplying the quoted facts are not preserved as separate incoming records in this source; publication cannot establish a direct reply or receipt date.

evidence.quote: Several of the facts given in the following letter from Fritz Müller
the important law or conclusion arrived at by the mathematician Delbœuf

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: Darwin responds to Nicols’s Nature question about rats gnawing water casks. He quotes Nicols’s carpenter report about thinning staves without making a hole, then supplies Wickham’s contrary historical account: water vessels were kept full to deter rats, whose holes would otherwise drain the cask. The contrast is narrow and evidential rather than a general animal-intelligence discussion.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published before 27 March 1879; XML bounds are 1809-01-01 to 1879-03-26. Nicols’s cited question appeared 13 March 1879, but the letter’s own publication date does not establish a physical receipt date.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin’s text frames and reports both accounts. Nicols and the unnamed carpenter, and Wickham’s recollection of naval service, remain attributed third-party testimony.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: Nicols’s Nature item is cited but no separate incoming letter is preserved; Wickham’s oral report is not an epistolary prompt.

evidence.quote: If any one could substantiate this it would have an important bearing on the question under consideration.
Capt. Wickham, when First Lieutenant on board H.M.S. Beagle, told me

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: Darwin publishes Sanderson’s account of Australian black or spotted sheep. He explains that coloured sheep were retained when useful for shepherding large unfenced flocks, then culled as fences and smaller flocks removed that utility; he relates the observation to reversion and selection. The long quotation is Sanderson’s, and the editorial note says the original letter, presumably to Darwin, has not been found.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published before 30 December 1880; XML bounds are 1809-01-01 to 1880-12-29. Publication establishes the outer date only; it does not date Sanderson’s composition or Darwin’s receipt.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin supplies the evolutionary framing; Sanderson’s quoted Australian experience is explicitly a separate voice. The original letter is unavailable.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The source itself records the missing Sanderson original, so there is no identifiable incoming endpoint for a direct reply.

evidence.quote: The following extract of a letter from Mr. Sanderson of Chislehurst, who permits me to publish it
as soon as coloured sheep ceased to be of use they were no longer allowed to grow up

record_reviews.source_kind: Darwin-authored outgoing published Nature item; complete preserved transcription
record_reviews.summary: Darwin publishes a Müller report from Santa Catharina dated 9 August on cold nights, upright young Pandanus leaves, older leaves damaged by exposure, and Oxalis leaflets hanging vertically in winter. Darwin says the seasonal difference in sleep is new to him and links the report to his radiation-protection view. The report is quoted through Darwin’s Nature item, not presented as a separate Müller record.
record_reviews.date_assessment: Published before 15 September 1881; XML bounds are 1809-01-01 to 1881-09-14. Müller’s internal 9 August dateline is distinct from Darwin’s later publication and any receipt date.
record_reviews.attribution_assessment: Darwin frames and quotes Müller; the plant observations belong to Müller. No Darwin annotation or editorial summary is treated as body prose.
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: The Müller letter of 9 August and any 10 August companion are cited in apparatus but not preserved as separate body endpoints here; no direct pair is proposed.

evidence.quote: Fritz Müller, in a letter to me from Sta. Catharina in Brazil, dated August 9
These young leaves, though of course the most tender, are still as fresh and green as before

unlocated_references.description: Galton paper/publication supplies the subject, but no distinct Galton incoming endpoint is preserved.
Huggins letter is announced and permitted for publication, but its body is not retained as a separate endpoint.
Wallace suggestion is reported without a preserved incoming letter.
Nature article is answered publicly; its author and a distinct incoming correspondence record are not identified.
Hague’s embedded report is present inside the publication, while a separate cover/prompt is absent.
Hague confirming letter is referred to but not retained in the body blocks.
Müller’s cited letter(s) are not preserved as separate body endpoints.
Nicols’s query is a prior Nature item and Wickham’s account is oral, not a preserved incoming letter.
Editorial apparatus explicitly says Sanderson’s original letter has not been found.
Müller’s 9 August letter is cited but not separately preserved in this record.

issues: All ten records are boundary probes with period_selection_eligible=false and open XML lower bounds of 1809; their supplied publication dates range from 1871 to 1881 and do not establish 1858–1859 eligibility.
Several records are publication composites containing quoted or reported third-party voices. Those voices remain attributed and are not treated as Darwin-authored incoming prompts.
